summary: Project Selene is a website that allows users to easily explore the entire moon and view it through 7 unique lenses: Optical / WAC, Elevation, Temperature, Slope Hazard, Solar Power %, H₂O Volatiles, DTE Comms, all in high resolution with special care being put into the lunar south pole, with important sites all labelled and having higher resolution. Views of the Earth-moon system and Earth-Sun system are also available. A lunar rover navigation planning and simulation tool has also been implemented with a plethora of pre existing rovers to choose from, or parameters to customize. All of this, at any point of time in history or in the future, with an indicator as to when the ideal time to execute a mission at a given point would be, all packaged into an intelligent 'mission readiness score'. I believe this has the potential to be a great learning tool and potential starting point for ambitious mission lunar mission planning.
details:
The best and fastest way to experience the project rather than a long essay is to visit it at https://selene-ops.vercel.app/

### What it does and how it works

Landing at the Lunar South Pole leaves thin margins across coupled physical constraints. Sunlight hits at zero to three degrees, so a bright ridge sits close to 25–45 K permanently shadowed craters holding water ice, while a 27.2-day optical libration cycle drops Earth behind crater rims for roughly half the month. I built SELENE OPS as a browser-based 3D lunar mission console that brings all of those variables onto one interactive globe.

Users can choose from 10 curated Artemis III, CLPS, ISRU, and historic landing sites, click anywhere on the Moon to drop a custom pin (or place coordinates relative to the Sun and Earth), and switch across seven real-time WebGL GLSL shader layers: LROC Optical/WAC Albedo, LOLA Elevation, Diviner Temperature (25–395 K), Slope Hazard, Solar Illumination Duty, Water-Ice Equivalent (wt% H2O), and Direct-to-Earth Visibility.

Under the hood, the terrain engine pairs a local South Polar Stereographic pyramid (IAU2000:30162) with live NASA Moon Trek OGC WMTS streaming. Around 78°S–90°S, custom shaders project vertices algebraically onto the polar plane to remove UV pinching and antimeridian seams, reading 16-bit RG-encoded NASA LOLA DEMs down to 35 m/px across Shackleton and 10 m/px (0.10 m vertical step) at Artemis Site 01. Everywhere else on the Moon, a quadtree streamer fetches 256×256 Moon Trek tiles (zoom z=4..8) on demand into a 4×4 RAM clipmap backed by a 192-tile LRU cache and parent-tile fallback.

For any past or future UTC epoch, the physics engine ray-marches 36 azimuths out to 140 km across the LOLA heightfield (including planetary curvature drop) to build a 360° horizon skyplot and 29.53-day synodic forecast, scoring each site out of 100 (GO >= 76, CAUTION, or automatic NO-GO on >12° slope, <150 W/m² eclipse, or total comm blackout) across Power (/30), Comms (/26), Slope (/20), Thermal (/14), and ISRU/Duty (/10). It also propagates five cislunar orbiters (LRO, Danuri, Queqiao-2, CAPSTONE NRHO, Lunar Pathfinder) via a Newton-Raphson Kepler solver across Lunar, South Pole, Earth–Moon, and Sun–Earth–Moon 3D views, and solves battery-aware rover routes on a pole-safe 43×31 gnomonic tangent-plane A* grid modeling 1.625 m/s² gravity, slope slip, downhill regeneration, and horizon-checked solar charging.

### Benefits

Lunar data usually sits split across separate maps, tables, and heavy desktop GIS tools. Putting everything on one 60 FPS WebGL globe makes tradeoffs immediate: move a landing pin a short distance off a ridge and solar duty, slope risk, temperature, and relay access update together. Streaming global Moon Trek tiles on demand avoids gigabyte downloads, and the subsystem score breakdown lets both engineers and newcomers audit why a site passes or fails in seconds.

### Intended impact

I built SELENE OPS to serve two groups at once. For mission planners, researchers, and students, it works as a fast browser sandbox to test landing ellipses, launch slips, relay passes, and rover paths before spinning up heavyweight simulation suites. For educators and the public, it turns Artemis and CLPS engineering constraints into an interactive 3D world anyone can explore.

### Creativity

Instead of burying users under static tables, I modeled the workspace like a real mission console mixed with familiar flight-sim tools. I also included historically improtant landing sites. It pairs Google Maps–style global tile streaming with high-precision polar relief displacement, adds KSP-style "Warp To" jumps straight to the next sunrise, DTE rise, or satellite pass, and runs rover routing in a distortion-free gnomonic tangent plane so paths behave cleanly right up to -90°. I also kept the workspace calm and readable with moveable, minimizable floating windows. This allows the user to understand a LOT about the moon very quickly in a very accessible manner.

### Factors I considered

I focused on physical accuracy, browser performance, and clear feedback. Real landers risk tipping past 8°–12° slopes, freezing in <95 K shadows, or losing Earth radio during libration lows, so every readiness rule and rover cost ties directly to local LOLA gradients and orbital geometry. At the same time, raw planetary rasters can easily hit gigabytes, so I encoded 16-bit polar elevations into compact RG PNG channels and capped live WMTS tiles in a 192-entry cache to hold smooth 60 FPS rendering on an ordinary laptop. Finally, I kept the UI uncluttered so every 100-point verdict shows the numbers behind it.

### Tools, coding languages, hardware, and software used

I built the application using TypeScript, GLSL, React 18, Three.js, @react-three/fiber, @react-three/drei, Tailwind CSS, Lucide icons, and Vite, paired with Python scripts (NumPy, Pillow, Matplotlib, python-pptx) for offline PDS/PGDA DEM processing and presentation visuals. My workflow used VS Code, Google Antigravity, Git/GitHub, Obsidian, PowerPoint, and Vercel on a standard consumer laptop and web browser. I handled the entire project ideation, mission design, physics modeling, and UX direction myself; AI coding agents in Google Antigravity assisted only with writing and scaffolding the implementation code, which I reviewed and verified.
